title: What games would you build if every NPC could remember, act on its own, stay in character and run instantly, free?only 16MB
author: tyn_21
selftext: I’m exploring a platform where NPCs independently notice events, remember what happened, form role bounded goals, take commands from players and carry consequences forward even between player conversations . The core intelligence runs locally, with no cloud calls or per-thought cost: one 16MB runtime can support 10 or 10,000 intelligent NPCs, so it is instant, offline capable, and does not get more expensive as the world scales. Developers define allowed actions, character roles, and story constraints; decisions are inspectable and testable. What types of games or game mechanics would this make possible for you, and would you build on a platform that offered it?

replies.author: EternalPump
replies.body: Just a bit of advice then: if you intend to pursue this work financially - you should file patents first. comments.author: Accomplished_Rock695
comments.body:
Every time someone pitches shit like this its some version of turning a bunch of AI inputs into vectors and then doing a bit of math. Which obviously scales well so then they make claims about how many agents it supports that sound bonkers.

Because it's a lie. It doesn't matter what one small slice of the framework does if all the runtime parts that talk to it take too long. Most of the quantized approaches are shit for l2 cache coherency so you end up burning a lot of actual time building the structs up to send to your planner.

Ppl have been pitching things like this for decades. It's never worked out.

replies.author: tyn_21
replies.body: That's not what this is at all there's no embedding math or quantized inference anywhere in the runtime, so the failure mode you're describing has nothing to attach to. It already runs at 60fps with a 2ms sim tick; paper and platform launching soon.

replies.author: Accomplished_Rock695
replies.body:
So you have a planner that somehow sync to game events without data passing?   
2ms sim tick for just your stack on a 16.6ms budget will be a go-no for most games. And a 2ms pix trace doesn't tell you anything about the non-call overhead from L2 work. 

You have to write the memory state somewhere. If you aren't supporting serialization then the entire stack is a joke. That requires information encoding. Whether you do it in integer or vector space doesn't matter, its still per actor encoding. 

Its fine. Live your dream. I've just seen this enough times over the last 3 decades of my career to not be impressed. Every single team eventually pitches something like this when they want to do a world sim. And every single time it has the same set of flaws. But, hey, build your open world shooter with 10k thinking and acting agents with short and long term memory and dynamically created outcomes with a robust streamed in/out planning layer and prove me wrong. Because it doesn't matter until you have an actual game running it.

replies.author: tyn_21
replies.body: To answer your question temperament is authored by the dev (a coward stays a coward), but attitudes are formed. Each character keeps their own memory of what specific people did to them, and trust and grudges build from that. So a betrayal wouldn't be scripted or random, it'd be an ally whose private ledger against you finally tipped. And since every decision writes a receipt, you could replay exactly which moments did it. A kill cam for the friendship

comments.author: EchoingAngel
comments.body: I already plan on my next game being basically X4-lite with the focus being on fleet combat (and the player being in it and that being the best choice they can make). It would be great if ships can have building character and there could be free agents in the world that can execute full chains of steps to be actual wild cards in the game world.

replies.author: tyn_21
replies.body: Every ship or captain can be a full character authored temperament plus accumulating memory, so a ship that survived three ambushes is warier than a fresh one, and a crew you abandoned remembers it. Your wild cards are what I'm most confident in: agents form intentions from what happened to them and pursue them through full chains of steps, but bounded by role, so a pirate wants plunder, a patrol captain wants order, and neither can break your rules to get it. Defections and vendettas emerge in the sim layer while combat stays entirely yours.
